title: Sampling & bias
examples: What is the difference between random and stratified sampling?
Can bias come from more than one place?
When should I use systematic sampling?

explain.say: Today we learn about how to pick good samples.
A random sample means every person has an equal chance.
For example, we could put every name in a hat to draw from.
Stratified sampling splits the group into smaller important groups first.
Then you take a random sample from each of those smaller groups.

faq.q: What is the best way to avoid bias in a survey?
faq.a: You should use a method that gives everyone a fair chance of being picked. Try to use random selection whenever possible.
asks: How do I stop my sample from being unfair?
What is the opposite of bias in sampling?

faq.q: When should I use stratified sampling instead of random sampling?
faq.a: Use it when you know the population has important subgroups. You need to make sure you sample from each group fairly.
asks: Does stratification always give better results?

faq.a: It means picking items at regular intervals from a list. For example, picking every tenth person on a list.
asks: How do I pick every nth item?

faq.a: This happens when some parts of the population are left out completely. For instance, only surveying people who use the internet.
asks: What is missing from my sample?
When am I excluding people by mistake?

faq.q: Can I combine different sampling methods?
faq.a: Yes, sometimes you might use stratification first, and then use random selection within those layers. It depends on the question.
asks: Can I mix up the methods?
Is there a mix of methods okay?

facts: Random sampling gives every member an equal chance of selection.
Stratified sampling ensures representation from key subgroups.
Systematic sampling selects participants at fixed intervals.
Bias occurs when the sample does not represent the whole population.

quiz.say: A school wants to know the opinion of students in Year 10 and Year 11. They take a random sample from each year group.
quiz.why: This method correctly ensures both year groups are represented proportionally.

wrong.0: This only samples students who are easy to reach, which is biased.
wrong.2: This might accidentally miss one of the year groups entirely.
wrong.3: This method relies on a list order that might not reflect the year groups.

quiz.say: A researcher surveys only students who attend the school library to gauge study habits.
quiz.why: The sample excludes students who do not use the library, creating bias.

wrong.0: This is too general; undercoverage is the specific type of bias here.
wrong.1: This bias happens when people choose to respond, not when they are excluded.
wrong.3: While related, undercoverage specifically means people are excluded from the sampling frame.

quiz.say: A list of 100 names is available. To select a sample, the researcher picks every 10th name starting from the 5th name.
quiz.why: This method uses a fixed interval, which is the definition of systematic sampling.

wrong.0: Cluster sampling involves selecting groups of items, not just following an interval.
wrong.2: Random sampling requires drawing numbers without a fixed pattern.
wrong.3: This method requires dividing the population into distinct groups first.
